paper.title: Making low alloy ultrahigh strength steel tough by high-density NiAl clusters
paper.paper_scope: A novel low alloy ultrahigh strength steel (1.3Al, with increased Ni and Al vs. the 0Al reference) is designed to introduce extremely high-density coherent NiAl clusters alongside submicron ε-carbides, and its precipitation behavior, dislocation regulation and multi-scale toughening mechanisms are systematically compared with the 0Al steel in the as-quenched and 180 °C/2 h tempered states.

alloys.description: Reference low alloy ultrahigh strength steel of the study (the baseline steel used for comparison with the NiAl-cluster-strengthened 1.3Al steel). Produced by vacuum induction melting plus vacuum arc remelting (VIM + VAR) into 500 kg ingots, forged into Φ170 mm billets.
alloys.alloys_notes: Composition reported as mass fraction (wt%) in Table 1. Only a residual Al content (0.03 wt%), so essentially free of NiAl-cluster-forming additions.

source.reason: Table 1 and the accompanying text define the two experimental steels as '0Al' and '1.3Al'; the 0Al steel is the baseline steel whose composition is the basis for increasing Ni and Al in the 1.3Al steel.

alloys.description: NiAl-cluster-strengthened low alloy ultrahigh strength steel, designed with increased Ni and Al relative to the 0Al steel to introduce an extremely high number density of coherent NiAl clusters together with ε-carbides. Produced by VIM + VAR into 500 kg ingots, forged into Φ170 mm billets.
alloys.alloys_notes: Composition reported as mass fraction (wt%) in Table 1. Ni and Al concentrations were appropriately increased over the 0Al steel to ensure sufficient NiAl content; contains extremely high-density NiAl clusters (~4.88 × 10^24 m^-3) after tempering.

source.reason: Table 1 and the text describe the 1.3Al steel as produced by raising Ni and Al based on the 0Al composition so as to achieve dual precipitation of ε-carbides and high-density NiAl clusters.

processes.description: Solution treatment at 970 °C for 1 h to dissolve carbides, followed by water quenching (as-quenched condition).
processes.processes_notes: This heat-treatment step was applied identically to both the 0Al and 1.3Al steels, so the process is alloy-independent and shared.

source.reason: The text states both steels underwent solution treatment at 970 °C for 1 h with water quenching after the step, and labels the resulting as-quenched states as 0Al,WQ and 1.3Al,WQ.

processes.description: Solution treatment at 970 °C for 1 h + water quenching, followed by low-temperature tempering at 180 °C for 2 h with water quenching.
processes.processes_notes: Applied identically to both steels; the tempered state follows the water-quenched (as-quenched) state. Labels written as 0Al,2 h and 1.3Al,2 h.

source.reason: The text describes tempering at 180 °C for 2 h after solution treatment with water quenching after each step, and names the tempered states 0Al,2 h and 1.3Al,2 h.
The as-quenched condition of the 0Al steel is designated 0Al,WQ and appears in the mechanical-properties table (WQ condition).
The 2 h tempered condition of the 0Al steel is designated 0Al,2 h (the tempered '2 h' entry in the mechanical-properties table).
The as-quenched condition of the 1.3Al steel is designated 1.3Al,WQ and appears in the mechanical-properties table (WQ condition).

The 2 h tempered condition of the 1.3Al steel is designated 1.3Al,2 h (the tempered '2 h' entry in the mechanical-properties table) and is the principal study object exhibiting high-density NiAl clusters.

unmapped_findings: Starting material fabrication (common to both steels): vacuum induction melting followed by vacuum arc remelting (VIM + VAR) to obtain 500 kg ingots, subsequently forged into Φ170 mm billets, with characterization specimens extracted from the quarter-radius position.
The paper mentions commercial low alloy ultrahigh strength steels 300 M, D6AC and Eglin in the introduction only as background/context, not as studied objects.
